blocks.prompt: The Fish That Cannot Run Away
blocks.text: A pufferfish is not a fast swimmer. It cannot race away from trouble. So it has another plan. When something scary comes close, the pufferfish gulps water into its belly. Its stretchy skin fills up. In a few seconds it is round like a ball, and much too big for a hungry mouth. The pufferfish has no ribs, so nothing gets in the way of its belly. When the scary fish gives up and leaves, the pufferfish spits the water back out. It goes back to being small. Then it goes looking for a crab to crunch.

blocks.prompt: The Slowest Fish in the Sea
blocks.text: A pufferfish is one of the slowest fish in the sea. Most fish push themselves along with a big tail. The pufferfish mostly waves its small side fins instead. That lets it hover and turn in tight places, but it cannot sprint. A slow fish in an ocean full of fast hunters needs a good trick. Here is the trick. The pufferfish gulps seawater into its stomach, which stretches like a balloon. Its skin stretches too. In about ten seconds the fish swells into a prickly ball two or three times its normal size. A hunter that was about to swallow a snack now has a spiky beach ball in its face. Most of them give up. Puffing up is hard work. It takes hours for the fish to feel normal again, so it only does it when it must. The rest of the day it hunts crabs and clams. Four of its teeth are fused into a hard beak, and it uses that beak to crack the shells open. Those teeth never stop growing, so all that crunching keeps them worn down to the right size.

4.title: The Fish That Puffs Up Like a Ball
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Fish That Puffs Up Like a Ball

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Family name Tetraodontidae means four teeth
No ribs and no pelvic bones
Inflates with water in under fifteen seconds
Carries tetrodotoxin, a nerve poison
Does not make the poison, it collects it
Farm-raised puffers on clean food are harmless

blocks.prompt: The Balloon That Fights Back
blocks.text: A pufferfish looks like a bad design. It is round, it is slow, and it swims by fluttering its side fins instead of driving with its tail. Almost anything in the ocean can catch it. So the pufferfish does not bother running. It has two defenses instead, and both are strange. The first is the one everybody knows. When threatened, the pufferfish gulps seawater into a stomach built to stretch. It has no ribs to block the expansion and no pelvic bones either, and its skin unfolds in pleats like an accordion. Within seconds a fish the size of your hand becomes a spiny ball the size of a grapefruit. A predator that opened its mouth for a snack suddenly cannot close it. Inflating is exhausting, though. Careful measurements found that a pufferfish can need hours to recover afterward, so this is a last resort, not a party trick. The second defense is worse for any predator that ignores the first. Most pufferfish carry tetrodotoxin in their skin, liver, and organs. It is one of the most powerful poisons known, and there is no antidote. The strange part is that the fish does not make it. Tetrodotoxin is built by ocean bacteria, and the pufferfish collects it by eating animals that carry those bacteria. Pufferfish raised in clean tanks on clean food grow up nearly harmless. The fish borrows its weapon from the sea, and if the sea stops supplying it, the weapon never arrives.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: About 120 species worldwide, some in fresh water
Swims with pectoral and dorsal fins, tail as rudder
Tetrodotoxin blocks the sodium gates in nerves
Roughly a thousand times deadlier than cyanide
Made by bacteria, stored by the fish
Served in Japan as fugu by licensed chefs only

blocks.prompt: The Fish That Borrows Its Poison
blocks.text: Nothing about the pufferfish suggests a survivor. It is slow, it is round, and it swims by rippling its pectoral and dorsal fins rather than driving with its tail. That design buys precision. A pufferfish can hover, back up, and pick a snail off a rock. What it cannot do is outrun anything. An animal that cannot flee has to solve the problem some other way, and the pufferfish solves it twice. The famous solution is inflation. A threatened pufferfish gulps seawater into a stomach that has traded most of its digestive work for pure elasticity, and the rest of the body simply gets out of the way. There are no ribs, no pelvic bones, and the skin unfolds in pleats. In well under a minute the fish doubles or triples in volume and stiffens into a prickly sphere. A predator whose mouth fit the fish a moment ago now has an object it cannot swallow. Biologists once assumed an inflated puffer was holding its breath. Careful measurements showed otherwise. It keeps breathing the whole time, but the effort is enormous, and a single inflation can take hours to recover from. Inflation is not a habit. It is an emergency. The second solution is chemical, and it is the reason people are careful around this fish. Most pufferfish carry tetrodotoxin, a nerve poison roughly a thousand times deadlier than cyanide by weight, concentrated in the liver, the ovaries, and the skin. It works by jamming shut the tiny sodium gates that nerve cells use to fire, so the signals simply stop. There is no antidote. Here is the twist. The fish is not the chemist. Tetrodotoxin is manufactured by ocean bacteria, and the pufferfish accumulates it through what it eats, storing a poison it did not invent and cannot be harmed by, because its own sodium gates are shaped so the molecule does not fit. Puffers reared in tanks on clean feed are essentially non-toxic, which is why some Japanese farms now raise them exactly that way. In Japan the fish is eaten as fugu. Chefs train for years and must hold a license to serve it, because the line between dinner and disaster is which organ the knife touches. It is a strange bargain on both sides. A fish that armed itself by eating, and a diner who pays extra for the risk it borrowed.

6.title: The Fish That Puffs Up Like a Ball
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Fish That Puffs Up Like a Ball

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Family Tetraodontidae, four fused teeth
Tail is a rudder, side fins do the work
Inflation measured in 2014: it keeps breathing
Tetrodotoxin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels
Its own channels are shaped to ignore the toxin
Torquigener albomaculosus builds sand circles

blocks.prompt: The Slow Fish That Borrowed a Weapon
blocks.text: Judged by the standards of a fish, the pufferfish is a catastrophe. Speed is the ocean's basic currency, and the pufferfish has almost none of it. Most fish generate thrust by sweeping a muscular tail. The pufferfish instead ripples its pectoral, dorsal, and anal fins, keeping the tail as a rudder and saving it for short bursts. The result is a swimmer of remarkable precision and very little pace. It can hover, reverse, and rotate on the spot to pluck a snail out of a crevice. What it cannot do is outrun a predator, and it never will. Evolution handed the pufferfish a body that guarantees it will be caught, and then handed it two ways of surviving the catching. The first is mechanical. A frightened pufferfish gulps seawater and pumps it into a stomach that has surrendered most of its digestive role in exchange for extraordinary elasticity. The rest of the body cooperates by getting out of the way. Pufferfish have no ribs and no pelvic girdle, and their skin is arranged in pleats that unfold like a paper fan. Within seconds the fish becomes a rigid, prickly sphere several times its resting volume, and a predator that had a meal in its mouth now has an object it cannot close its jaws around. For a long time the assumption was that an inflated pufferfish holds its breath. Measurements published in 2014 showed the opposite. It goes on taking up oxygen the entire time it is inflated, but the performance is metabolically brutal, and recovery can take hours. Inflation is not a trick the fish enjoys. It is the alarm it pulls when everything else has failed. The second defense is chemical and considerably less sporting. Most pufferfish tissue carries tetrodotoxin, among the most potent poisons known, roughly a thousand times more lethal by weight than cyanide, concentrated in the liver, the ovaries, and the skin. Tetrodotoxin works by plugging the voltage-gated sodium channels that nerve and muscle cells use to fire. Blocked, the nerves fall silent and the muscles stop answering. There is no antidote. Treatment is life support until the body clears the toxin on its own. The surprise is that the pufferfish is not the manufacturer. Tetrodotoxin is synthesized by marine bacteria, and the fish acquires it up the food chain, concentrating a poison it neither invented nor can be hurt by, since its own sodium channels are shaped so the molecule does not fit. Pufferfish raised in tanks on clean feed grow up nearly toxin free, which is not a curiosity but a business. Japanese farms sell low-toxin fugu on exactly that principle. The fish is a warehouse, not a factory. That distinction matters more than it sounds. A poison you build is yours. A poison you borrow depends on a supply chain of bacteria, prey, and habitat, and humans are busy rearranging all three. Then, occasionally, a pufferfish does something no defense explains. Off the Japanese island of Amami Oshima, divers in 1995 began finding perfect circular patterns carved into the seabed, about seven feet across, ridged and grooved like a sand rose. Nobody knew what made them. The answer, confirmed in 2014, was a male pufferfish barely five inches long, working for roughly a week, swimming and flapping to plow the ridges and then decorating them with fragments of shell. The species had never been formally described. The structure is a nest. Females inspect the pattern and lay their eggs in the fine sediment at the middle, where the ridges appear to soften the current. So the slowest fish in the sea, armed with a stomach and a borrowed poison, is also an architect. Almost nothing about this animal makes sense until you accept that it was never trying to be fast.
